Thomas's eyes, set in a face too young to belong to him but wearing them anyway, that particular shade of grey like the winter sea, like the sky before snow, like every ghost Imogen had been trying not to see for twelve years.

The girl—Mara—stood on the doorstep wearing a coat too thin for the Welsh coast and carrying a backpack that looked heavy. Her dark hair was pulled back in a ponytail that the wind had already started destroying. She was taller than Imogen had imagined. Sixteen but already taller, already carrying herself with that careful determination of someone who's traveled a long way alone and isn't sure of their welcome.

"You're Imogen, right?" Her voice was steadier than it had been on the phone. "Imogen Williams?"

Imogen couldn't speak. Could only stare at those grey eyes in that young face, at Thomas looking back at her through his daughter's face, at the past refusing to stay locked in a blue tin where it couldn't reach her.

"Yes," she managed.

"I'm Mara. I think you're my aunt."

The wind pushed cold air through the open door. Somewhere behind Mara the tide was coming in again, Imogen could hear it, that soft persistent claiming. The girl shifted her weight, the backpack heavy on her shoulder, and her eyes—Thomas's eyes—watched Imogen with something that looked like hope and fear and desperate determination all counting up to a sum Imogen couldn't calculate.

"I know," Imogen said. "I know who you are."

Mara's shoulders dropped a fraction. "Can I come in? I took the bus from Cornwall. Six hours."

Imogen should say no. Should close the door. Should protect herself from this girl who looked at her with Thomas's eyes and asked questions Imogen couldn't answer. Should count to a hundred and send her away before the arithmetic shattered completely.

She stepped aside.

Mara hesitated for just a moment, then walked past her into the house. Into the kitchen. Into Imogen's carefully constructed solitude that was suddenly full of Thomas's daughter and Thomas's eyes and the smell of a stranger's shampoo and the sound of a backpack being set down on tiles that numbered exactly one thousand one hundred and seventy-six.

Imogen closed the door.

The silence stretched between them, awkward and heavy. Mara stood in the middle of the kitchen, taking it in—the cold soup pot, the three cups of untouched tea, the photograph of Imogen's mother above the stove, the table with its—

Mara's eyes went to the blue tin. To the opened letter beside it. To the eleven white envelopes still waiting.

"What are those?" she asked.

Imogen's hands found each other, fingers lacing tight. "They're private."

"Are they from him?"

"Yes."

Mara stared at the letters. At the tin. At the single opened envelope lying beside them. Her jaw worked like she was trying to count something too, trying to make sense of what she was seeing.

"How many?"

"Twelve."

"Twelve." Mara's voice went quiet. "I don't have anything. No letters. He left when I was three. Died when I was four. I don't remember him except in pieces."

"I just want to know where he's buried. Maybe—maybe there's something in the letters? An address?"

"I only opened one. Last night. I don't know what the others say."

"So open them."

"It's not that simple."

"Yes it is." Mara's voice sharpened. "They're just letters."

"I can't."

"Why not?"

Because opening them meant reading his words. Meant hearing his voice. Meant letting him forgive her when she didn't deserve forgiveness. Meant breaking the arithmetic that had kept her safe for twelve years.

Mara shook her head. "Everyone says it's complicated. I think complicated is just what adults say when they don't want to deal with something."

Mara nodded slowly. "I'm glad he had you. Even if it got complicated."

Three digits away from facing her sister's anger and her sister's grief and the twelve years of being too careful to ask.

Imogen's thumb hovered over the call button.

She counted to ten. Then twenty. Then fifty.

At one hundred she put the phone down.

Tomorrow.

Tomorrow.

It just came, inevitable and indifferent, covering everything.

The words settled in Imogen's chest, heavy and terrible and true. She was Thomas's sister. This girl was Thomas's daughter. They were connected by blood and grief and twenty years of letters that had gone unanswered.

"I'll find out where he's buried," Imogen said. "I promise."

Mara smiled. Small and tired and grateful. "Okay."

Imogen closed the door and stood in the hallway, her forehead pressed against the wall, counting her breaths. In for four. Hold for seven. Out for eight. The arithmetic wasn't working but she kept trying anyway because trying was all she had left.

Tomorrow she would call Eluned. Tomorrow she would ask the question she should have asked twelve years ago. Tomorrow she would try to be something other than frozen.

But tonight Mara was sleeping in Thomas's old room, and the blue tin was still open on the kitchen table, and somewhere outside the tide was coming in again without asking anyone whether they were ready, and Imogen stood in the dark hallway counting the ways her careful life had come apart in the space of two days.

Twelve letters. One niece. Zero answers. The equation refused to balance.

She went to her room. Got the spare bedding from the closet. Brought it to Mara's door and knocked softly. Mara opened it, still wearing her jeans but with her shoes off, her hair loose now around her shoulders.

"Blankets," Imogen said. "It gets cold at night."

"Thanks."

Imogen handed them over. Mara took them and set them on the bed, then stood there in the doorway, not quite ready to close the door.

"Did you love him? My dad?"

The question was so simple. So impossible.

"Yes," Imogen said. "Very much."

"What was he like?"

Imogen thought of Thomas teaching her to count the distance of lightning strikes. Thomas teaching her to drive on the coastal road. Thomas laughing when she got something wrong and patient when she was scared and always, always reaching back for her even when she couldn't reach forward to meet him.

"He was kind. And stubborn. And he believed things could be fixed if you just tried hard enough."

"He was wrong about that, wasn't he?" Mara's voice was very quiet.

"I don't know. Maybe he was right and I just never tried hard enough."

Mara nodded slowly. "I'm glad he had you. Even if it got complicated."

She closed the door before Imogen could respond. Before Imogen could tell her that loving Thomas had never been complicated at all. It was the easiest thing in the world. It was everything else—the guilt and the grief and the arithmetic of trying to survive when the person you loved most had forgiven you and you couldn't forgive yourself—that was complicated.

Imogen went back to the kitchen. The blue tin was still there. The eleven unopened letters were still waiting. She should close the tin. Should put the letters away. Should try to sleep.

Instead she sat at the table and picked up her phone.

Eluned's number was right there. Three digits away from knowing where Thomas was buried. Three digits away from giving Mara what she'd traveled six hours on a bus to find.

Three digits away from facing her sister's anger and her sister's grief and the twelve years of being too careful to ask.

Imogen's thumb hovered over the call button.

She counted to ten. Then twenty. Then fifty.

At one hundred she put the phone down.

Not tonight. She couldn't do it tonight. Tomorrow. She'd call tomorrow when she was steadier, when she'd had time to find the words, when she could explain to Eluned why she needed this information now after twelve years of not needing it.

Tomorrow.

She stood and walked to the window. The tide was in now, covering the flats, erasing the grey mud and the rock pools and all the careful patterns she'd counted a thousand times. The water was dark under the dark sky, barely visible except where the house lights caught it.

Upstairs in Thomas's old room, Mara was probably asleep by now. Or lying awake in a strange bed in a stranger's house, wondering if this trip had been worth it, if her aunt would actually help her or if she'd just found another adult with complications and excuses and no answers.

Imogen counted her breaths. One. Two. Three. The numbers fell into the darkness like stones into water, like all the words she'd never said, like twenty years of letters she'd never answered.

Tomorrow she would call Eluned. Tomorrow she would try to find out where Thomas was buried. Tomorrow she would open another letter, and another, until she'd read all twelve and knew what Thomas had spent twenty years trying to tell her.

Tomorrow.

But tonight she stood at the window with her phone in her hand and the arithmetic failing and a girl with grey eyes sleeping in the room that used to belong to her brother, and outside the tide kept coming in the way it always did. It didn't count. It didn't measure. It didn't ask anyone if they were ready or if they'd solved the equation or if they'd forgiven themselves yet.

It just came, inevitable and indifferent, covering everything.

# Chapter 5 — Three Women

The house made different sounds with someone else in it. Footsteps overhead—soft, careful, trying not to wake her. Water running in the bathroom. The creak of a floorboard Imogen had learned to avoid but Mara didn't know about yet.

Imogen lay in bed counting the sounds. Seven footsteps. Eleven seconds of running water. Three creaks.

She'd been awake since five, when the grey light started filtering through the curtains and her body remembered that daylight meant getting up, meant functioning, meant performing the arithmetic of a normal day. But there was nothing normal about a sixteen-year-old girl sleeping in Thomas's old room. Nothing normal about the blue tin still open on the kitchen table. Nothing normal about the promise she'd made to call Eluned and ask where Thomas was buried.

The water stopped. More footsteps. Silence.

Imogen counted to one hundred, then got up.

The kitchen was exactly as she'd left it—the blue tin on the table, the first letter beside it, the eleven unopened envelopes waiting. The photograph of her mother watched from above the stove. The tiles were still grey and white and numbered exactly one thousand one hundred and seventy-six, though counting them this morning didn't bring the same relief it usually did.

She filled the kettle. Put bread in the toaster. Set out two cups, two plates. The arithmetic of breakfast for two people instead of one.

Mara appeared in the doorway wearing the same jeans from yesterday and a different shirt, her dark hair wet from the shower. Her grey eyes—Thomas's grey eyes—took in the kitchen, the careful preparation, Imogen's hands arranging things just so.

"Good morning," Mara said.

"Morning. Did you sleep?"

"Some. The bed's comfortable. Thank you."

The politeness was careful, practiced. Both of them performing normal. Both of them pretending this wasn't strange.

"Tea?" Imogen asked.

"Please. Can I help?"

"It's fine. The kettle's almost—" The kettle clicked off. "Ready."

Imogen poured. Her hands were steady. She counted the seconds of pouring. Four for each cup. Eight total. The steam rose in identical patterns, predictable and safe.

They sat at the table. The blue tin sat between them like a third presence, impossible to ignore. Mara's eyes kept going to it, then away, then back.

"Did you sleep?" Mara asked, echoing Imogen's question but making it mean something different. Did you sleep or did you stay awake thinking about the letters, about your promise, about how to fix this?

"Some," Imogen said, echoing Mara's answer.

The toast popped. Imogen got up, buttered it, brought it back. Mara took a piece and ate it in small, careful bites. Sixteen. Still a child in some ways, still learning how to take up space in the world.

"I texted my mum," Mara said. "Told her we got to London fine. That I forgot my charger."

"Three days?"

"That's when the trip ends. Sunday night."

Today was Friday. Three days. Seventy-two hours. Four thousand three hundred and twenty minutes. The numbers should have been comforting but they just felt like a countdown to something Imogen wasn't ready for.

"What happens Sunday night?"

Mara shrugged. "I go home. Or I tell her the truth. Haven't decided yet."

Her voice was casual but her hands were tight around the tea cup, her knuckles white. Imogen recognized that grip. That was someone holding on because letting go meant falling apart.

"You could call her. Tell her you're safe."

"She'd make me come home."

"She's probably worried."

"She's always worried. That's what she does." Mara set down the cup. "I'm not going back until I know where he is. I need to see where they buried him."

The determination in her voice was so much like Thomas it hurt. Thomas deciding to leave Wales. Thomas deciding to keep writing even when Imogen never wrote back. Thomas deciding to rebuild the boat from their childhood even though he'd never finished it.

"I'll call Eluned this morning," Imogen said. "I promise."

Mara nodded. Looked at the blue tin. "Are you going to open another one?"

"I don't know."

"Why did you open the first one? After twelve years, why now?"

Because you called. Because your voice asking about Thomas broke something in Imogen's careful architecture. Because the arithmetic of avoidance had finally accumulated enough weight to collapse under itself.

"It was time," Imogen said, which wasn't an answer but was all she had.

Her phone buzzed on the counter. They both looked at it. Imogen's stomach tightened. It could be the school. Could be Eluned. Could be nothing important, just a reminder or a notification, but her body responded to it the way you respond to a fire alarm—immediate, visceral, counting the seconds until it stops.

She crossed to the phone. Checked it.

Five missed calls from Eluned. Three from yesterday. Two from this morning. No messages. Just the calls, insistent and unanswered.

"Is it her?" Mara asked. "Your sister?"

"Yes."

"Are you going to call her back?"

Imogen looked at the phone in her hand. At the five missed calls that were really five chances to ask the question she should have asked twelve years ago. Five chances to find out where Thomas was buried. Five chances to stop being the sister who was too careful to fall apart.

"Yes," she said. "I will."

But not yet. Not with Mara watching. Not with the blue tin open and the morning still too new and her counting already spiraling past fifty, sixty, seventy because Eluned's calls meant Eluned was worried or angry or both and Imogen didn't know how to face that yet.

The sound of tires on gravel made them both look toward the window.

Imogen knew that sound. Knew the particular crunch of Eluned's car pulling up to the house. Knew what it meant that Eluned hadn't waited for Imogen to call back but had come instead.

"Is that—" Mara started.

"Yes."

Imogen set down her phone. Her heart was beating too fast, that familiar flutter of panic when things moved faster than she could count, faster than she could control. She pressed her hands flat against the table. One thousand one hundred and seventy-six tiles. The blue tin. Eleven unopened letters. One niece with grey eyes. One sister pulling up outside.

The car door slammed.

Footsteps on the gravel. Quick, determined. Not the careful footsteps of someone who's uncertain. The footsteps of someone who's decided something and come to make it happen.

Mara stood. "Should I—"

"Stay." Imogen's voice came out sharper than she meant it. "Please. Just stay."

The knock came. Three sharp raps on the door.

Imogen didn't count her steps this time. Just crossed to the door and opened it.

Eluned stood on the doorstep wearing her work coat and her brown eyes already searching past Imogen into the house, looking for whatever had made Imogen ignore five phone calls. Her hair was pulled back, still damp like she'd come straight from the shower. Her jaw was tight the way it got when she was trying to hold something in.

"You didn't answer," Eluned said.

"I know. I was going to call—"

"I've been worried. After the other night, after what I said, I thought—" She stopped. Her eyes had found Mara standing in the kitchen doorway. "Who is that?"

The question came out flat. Careful. Eluned's voice when she already knew the answer but needed to hear it said aloud.

Imogen's mouth went dry. "Her name is Mara."

"Mara."

"Thomas's daughter."

Eluned went very still. Her eyes moved from Mara to Imogen and back again, taking it in—the girl in the kitchen, the overnight bag visible in the hallway, the two cups on the table, the whole impossible situation that Imogen had created without asking, without warning, without thinking about what it would do to Eluned to walk in and find Thomas's daughter here.

"When did she—"

"Yesterday. She called, then she came. She had nowhere else to go."

Eluned's jaw tightened further. She stepped inside, closed the door behind her with careful precision. Walked past Imogen into the kitchen where Mara stood very straight, very still, trying to look older than sixteen and not quite managing it.

"Hello," Mara said. Her voice was steady but her hands had found each other, fingers lacing tight. "I'm Mara Penrose. You're Eluned?"

"I am." Eluned set her bag on the counter. Took off her coat. Each movement deliberate, controlled. "Does your mother know you're here?"

"She thinks I'm in London. School trip."

"So that's a no."

"I needed to find out where my dad is buried. No one would tell me."

Eluned looked at Imogen. "And you let her stay."

It wasn't a question. It was an accusation wrapped in four quiet words.

"She had nowhere to go," Imogen said. "She came all the way from Cornwall—"

"So you brought her into this." Eluned gestured at the table, at the blue tin, at the letters spread across Imogen's carefully constructed solitude. "After everything I said the other night. After I told you those letters would destroy you. You opened one and then brought his daughter here to witness it."

"I didn't plan—"

"You never plan. You just react. You just let things happen to you and then count your way through the wreckage."

The words landed like blows. Mara shifted her weight, uncomfortable, caught in the middle of something she didn't understand.

"I should go," Mara said quietly. "I can find somewhere else—"

"No." Imogen's voice surprised her, sharp and certain. "You're staying. I promised I'd help you and I will."

Eluned laughed, but there was no humor in it. "You promised. Like you promised to deal with the letters twelve years ago? Like you promised to talk to me about Thomas before now?"

"That's not fair."

"Fair?" Eluned's control cracked, just for a moment, her voice rising. "You want to talk about fair? I handled everything when he died. The funeral, the arrangements, the phone calls to his ex-wife telling her that Thomas was gone and yes, we'd make sure Mara was taken care of financially but no, Imogen wasn't in a state to meet her. I handled all of it while you stayed here counting tiles and refusing to open his letters. And now you've dragged this girl into it because she asked you a question you should have asked me twelve years ago."

The silence that followed was absolute. Mara's face had gone white. Imogen couldn't breathe, couldn't count, couldn't do anything except stand there with the truth of Eluned's words settling into her chest like stones.

"I'm sorry," Imogen whispered.

"Sorry doesn't help her." Eluned nodded at Mara. "Sorry doesn't tell her where her father is buried. Sorry doesn't give her twelve years back."

"Then tell me." Mara's voice cut through the tension, young and desperate and demanding. "Please. You know where he is. Just tell me."

Eluned looked at her for a long moment. At Thomas's grey eyes in Mara's young face. At the daughter who'd come looking for a father she barely remembered.

"Sit down," Eluned said finally. "All of us. Sit."

It was a command, not a request. They sat—Eluned and Imogen on one side of the table, Mara on the other, the blue tin between them like something that could explode if handled wrong.

Eluned folded her hands on the table. Breathed in. Breathed out. When she spoke again her voice was calmer, more controlled, but Imogen could see the cost of that control in the tightness around her eyes.

"I'll tell you where he's buried. But first we need to talk about what happens next."

"I just want to visit his grave," Mara said. "That's all."

"Nothing is ever that simple." Eluned looked at Imogen. "She can stay three days? That's when her school trip ends?"

Imogen nodded.

"Fine. Three days. But if she stays, you open the letters. All of them. No more hiding behind arithmetic and excuses."

"Eluned—"

"All of them, Imogen. That's the deal. She wants to know about her father, and those letters are the only way she'll hear his voice. You want to know where he's buried, and I'll tell you. But you don't get to keep hiding. Not anymore. Not with her here."

The demand hung in the air between them. Imogen looked at the eleven unopened letters. At Mara's desperate hope. At Eluned's exhausted fury.

"I can't," Imogen said.

"Yes you can. You already opened one. You can open the rest."

"They're private—"

"He's been private for twenty years." Eluned's voice was gentle now, which made it worse. "Read them. Let us hear what he had to say. Maybe it'll help."

"Help with what?"

"Letting him go."

The words settled into the silence. Mara was watching Imogen with Thomas's eyes. Eluned was watching her with their mother's. And Imogen was trapped between them with eleven letters she'd spent twelve years avoiding and a promise she didn't know how to keep.

"One letter," she heard herself say. "I'll open one more. The second one. Today."

"All of them," Eluned insisted.

"I can't do all of them at once. One at a time. One per day until they're gone."

Eluned considered this. "Fine. One per day. Starting now."

She reached across the table and pushed the blue tin toward Imogen.

"Now?" Imogen's voice cracked.

"Right now. Both of us here. Both of us listening." Eluned looked at Mara. "Your father was my brother too. You're not the only one with questions."

Mara nodded slowly. "Then why won't anyone answer them?"

"Because some answers hurt more than the questions." Eluned's eyes were bright. "But maybe it's time to hurt a little if it means we stop hiding."

Imogen looked at the tin. At the second envelope, dated six months after the first. Six months of Thomas waiting for an answer. Six months of silence accumulating into years, into decades, into a lifetime of words she'd refused to hear.

Her hands shook as she reached for it.

The envelope was lighter than the first. Thinner. The paper had yellowed at the edges where twenty years had touched it. The postmark was from Cornwall, from a town Imogen had never visited even though Thomas had lived there for two decades. His handwriting on the front—her name in that impatient slant, the 'g' diving below the line like a gull diving below the water.

She counted to ten. Then twenty. Then thirty.

Eluned waited. Mara waited. The whole kitchen waited, heavy with the weight of words about to be spoken.

At fifty, Imogen stopped counting and opened the letter.

The paper tore along the seal. She pulled out a single page, folded once. Thomas's handwriting covered both sides—smaller than the first letter, more cramped, like he'd had more to say than space to say it in.

"Read it aloud," Eluned said quietly. "Both of you should hear it."

Imogen's throat closed. "It's private—"

"He's been private for twenty years. Read it."

Imogen looked at the first line. At Thomas's younger voice speaking across decades of silence. Her lips moved, counting the words before she could make herself say them aloud.

"Read it," Eluned said again.

Imogen read.

"Dear Imogen,

I know you probably won't answer this letter either, but I'm writing anyway because not writing feels like giving up and I'm not ready to give up on you yet.

It's been six months since I wrote the first letter. Six months in Cornwall, which is beautiful but lonely. I've got work at a boat yard—restoration mostly, old fishing vessels and pleasure boats that people bring in more broken than whole. The work is good. Keeps my hands busy. Keeps me from thinking too much about Wales, about you and Eluned, about everything I left behind.

The town is small. Everyone knows everyone. They know I'm from Wales, that I left home, but they don't ask too many questions and I don't offer too many answers. That suits me fine.

I've got a flat above the chandlery. Two rooms and a view of the harbor. There's a spare room if you ever wanted to visit. I know you won't, but I'm telling you anyway. The door's open. It'll stay open.

I'm not angry anymore. I was for a while after I left—angry at you, at Eluned, at Mum for dying, at myself for not being able to fix it. But anger takes too much energy and I didn't have enough left after the leaving.

What I have now is hope. Stupid, probably. But I hope you'll write back. Hope you'll tell me how you are, what you're doing, if you've forgiven yourself yet for something that was never your fault.

I don't blame you. I told you that in the last letter but I'll say it again because I don't think you believed me. It wasn't your fault. The rain, the road, the way Mum didn't put her seatbelt on, the way I told you to go faster—none of that was your fault. But you've made it your fault anyway and I can't fix that from Cornwall. Only you can fix that.

I miss you. I miss my sister who used to count the stars with me. I miss the way you'd get so focused on a problem you'd forget to eat. I miss having someone who knew me before I became the person who left.

If you ever change your mind, the address is on the envelope. The spare room is waiting. I'll keep writing even if you never write back.

Imogen's voice broke on the last word. She set the letter down with shaking hands. Across the table, Mara's face was wet with tears. Beside her, Eluned had her eyes closed, her jaw tight.

# Chapter 5 — Three Women

The house made different sounds with someone else in it. Footsteps overhead—soft, careful, trying not to wake her. Water running in the bathroom. The creak of a floorboard Imogen had learned to avoid but Mara didn't know about yet.

Imogen lay in bed counting the sounds. Seven footsteps. Eleven seconds of running water. Three creaks.

She'd been awake since five, when the grey light started filtering through the curtains and her body remembered that daylight meant getting up, meant functioning, meant performing the arithmetic of a normal day. But there was nothing normal about a sixteen-year-old girl sleeping in Thomas's old room. Nothing normal about the blue tin still open on the kitchen table. Nothing normal about the promise she'd made to call Eluned and ask where Thomas was buried.

The water stopped. More footsteps. Silence.

Imogen counted to one hundred, then got up.

The kitchen was exactly as she'd left it—the blue tin on the table, the first letter beside it, the eleven unopened envelopes waiting. The photograph of her mother watched from above the stove. The tiles were still grey and white and numbered exactly one thousand one hundred and seventy-six, though counting them this morning didn't bring the same relief it usually did.

She filled the kettle. Put bread in the toaster. Set out two cups, two plates. The arithmetic of breakfast for two people instead of one.

Mara appeared in the doorway wearing the same jeans from yesterday and a different shirt, her dark hair wet from the shower. Her grey eyes—Thomas's grey eyes—took in the kitchen, the careful preparation, Imogen's hands arranging things just so.

"Good morning," Mara said.

"Morning. Did you sleep?"

"Some. The bed's comfortable. Thank you."

The politeness was careful, practiced. Both of them performing normal. Both of them pretending this wasn't strange.

"Tea?" Imogen asked.

"Please. Can I help?"

"It's fine. The kettle's almost—" The kettle clicked off. "Ready."

Imogen poured. Her hands were steady. She counted the seconds of pouring. Four for each cup. Eight total. The steam rose in identical patterns, predictable and safe.

They sat at the table. The blue tin sat between them like a third presence, impossible to ignore. Mara's eyes kept going to it, then away, then back.

"Did you sleep?" Mara asked, echoing Imogen's question but making it mean something different. Did you sleep or did you stay awake thinking about the letters, about your promise, about how to fix this?

"Some," Imogen said, echoing Mara's answer.

The toast popped. Imogen got up, buttered it, brought it back. Mara took a piece and ate it in small, careful bites. Sixteen. Still a child in some ways, still learning how to take up space in the world.

"I texted my mum," Mara said. "Told her we got to London fine. That I forgot my charger."

"Three days?"

"That's when the trip ends. Sunday night."

Today was Friday. Three days. Seventy-two hours. Four thousand three hundred and twenty minutes. The numbers should have been comforting but they just felt like a countdown to something Imogen wasn't ready for.

"What happens Sunday night?"

Mara shrugged. "I go home. Or I tell her the truth. Haven't decided yet."

Her voice was casual but her hands were tight around the tea cup, her knuckles white. Imogen recognized that grip. That was someone holding on because letting go meant falling apart.

"You could call her. Tell her you're safe."

"She'd make me come home."

"She's probably worried."

"She's always worried. That's what she does." Mara set down the cup. "I'm not going back until I know where he is. I need to see where they buried him."

The determination in her voice was so much like Thomas it hurt. Thomas deciding to leave Wales. Thomas deciding to keep writing even when Imogen never wrote back. Thomas deciding to rebuild the boat from their childhood even though he'd never finished it.

"I'll call Eluned this morning," Imogen said. "I promise."

Mara nodded. Looked at the blue tin. "Are you going to open another one?"

"I don't know."

"Why did you open the first one? After twelve years, why now?"

Because you called. Because your voice asking about Thomas broke something in Imogen's careful architecture. Because the arithmetic of avoidance had finally accumulated enough weight to collapse under itself.

"It was time," Imogen said, which wasn't an answer but was all she had.

Her phone buzzed on the counter. They both looked at it. Imogen's stomach tightened. It could be the school. Could be Eluned. Could be nothing important, just a reminder or a notification, but her body responded to it the way you respond to a fire alarm—immediate, visceral, counting the seconds until it stops.

She crossed to the phone. Checked it.

Five missed calls from Eluned. Three from yesterday. Two from this morning. No messages. Just the calls, insistent and unanswered.

"Is it her?" Mara asked. "Your sister?"

"Yes."

"Are you going to call her back?"

Imogen looked at the phone in her hand. At the five missed calls that were really five chances to ask the question she should have asked twelve years ago. Five chances to find out where Thomas was buried. Five chances to stop being the sister who was too careful to fall apart.

"Yes," she said. "I will."

But not yet. Not with Mara watching. Not with the blue tin open and the morning still too new and her counting already spiraling past fifty, sixty, seventy because Eluned's calls meant Eluned was worried or angry or both and Imogen didn't know how to face that yet.

The sound of tires on gravel made them both look toward the window.

Imogen knew that sound. Knew the particular crunch of Eluned's car pulling up to the house. Knew what it meant that Eluned hadn't waited for Imogen to call back but had come instead.

"Is that—" Mara started.

"Yes."

Imogen set down her phone. Her heart was beating too fast, that familiar flutter of panic when things moved faster than she could count, faster than she could control. She pressed her hands flat against the table. One thousand one hundred and seventy-six tiles. The blue tin. Eleven unopened letters. One niece with grey eyes. One sister pulling up outside.

The car door slammed.

Footsteps on the gravel. Quick, determined. Not the careful footsteps of someone who's uncertain. The footsteps of someone who's decided something and come to make it happen.

Mara stood. "Should I—"

"Stay." Imogen's voice came out sharper than she meant it. "Please. Just stay."

The knock came. Three sharp raps on the door.

Imogen didn't count her steps this time. Just crossed to the door and opened it.

Eluned stood on the doorstep wearing her work coat and her brown eyes already searching past Imogen into the house, looking for whatever had made Imogen ignore five phone calls. Her hair was pulled back, still damp like she'd come straight from the shower. Her jaw was tight the way it got when she was trying to hold something in.

"You didn't answer," Eluned said.

"I know. I was going to call—"

"I've been worried. After the other night, after what I said, I thought—" She stopped. Her eyes had found Mara standing in the kitchen doorway. "Who is that?"

The question came out flat. Careful. Eluned's voice when she already knew the answer but needed to hear it said aloud.

Imogen's mouth went dry. "Her name is Mara."

"Mara."

"Thomas's daughter."

Eluned went very still. Her eyes moved from Mara to Imogen and back again, taking it in—the girl in the kitchen, the overnight bag visible in the hallway, the two cups on the table, the whole impossible situation that Imogen had created without asking, without warning, without thinking about what it would do to Eluned to walk in and find Thomas's daughter here.

"When did she—"

"Yesterday. She called, then she came. She had nowhere else to go."

Eluned's jaw tightened further. She stepped inside, closed the door behind her with careful precision. Walked past Imogen into the kitchen where Mara stood very straight, very still, trying to look older than sixteen and not quite managing it.

"Hello," Mara said. Her voice was steady but her hands had found each other, fingers lacing tight. "I'm Mara Penrose. You're Eluned?"

"I am." Eluned set her bag on the counter. Took off her coat. Each movement deliberate, controlled. "Does your mother know you're here?"

"She thinks I'm in London. School trip."

"So that's a no."

"I needed to find out where my dad is buried. No one would tell me."

Eluned looked at Imogen. "And you let her stay."

It wasn't a question. It was an accusation wrapped in four quiet words.

"She had nowhere to go," Imogen said. "She came all the way from Cornwall—"

"So you brought her into this." Eluned gestured at the table, at the blue tin, at the letters spread across Imogen's carefully constructed solitude. "After everything I said the other night. After I told you those letters would destroy you. You opened one and then brought his daughter here to witness it."

"I didn't plan—"

"You never plan. You just react. You just let things happen to you and then count your way through the wreckage."

The words landed like blows. Mara shifted her weight, uncomfortable, caught in the middle of something she didn't understand.

"I should go," Mara said quietly. "I can find somewhere else—"

"No." Imogen's voice surprised her, sharp and certain. "You're staying. I promised I'd help you and I will."

Eluned laughed, but there was no humor in it. "You promised. Like you promised to deal with the letters twelve years ago? Like you promised to talk to me about Thomas before now?"

"That's not fair."

"Fair?" Eluned's control cracked, just for a moment, her voice rising. "You want to talk about fair? I handled everything when he died. The funeral, the arrangements, the phone calls to his ex-wife telling her that Thomas was gone and yes, we'd make sure Mara was taken care of financially but no, Imogen wasn't in a state to meet her. I handled all of it while you stayed here counting tiles and refusing to open his letters. And now you've dragged this girl into it because she asked you a question you should have asked me twelve years ago."

The silence that followed was absolute. Mara's face had gone white. Imogen couldn't breathe, couldn't count, couldn't do anything except stand there with the truth of Eluned's words settling into her chest like stones.

"I'm sorry," Imogen whispered.

"Sorry doesn't help her." Eluned nodded at Mara. "Sorry doesn't tell her where her father is buried. Sorry doesn't give her twelve years back."

"Then tell me." Mara's voice cut through the tension, young and desperate and demanding. "Please. You know where he is. Just tell me."

Eluned looked at her for a long moment. At Thomas's grey eyes in Mara's young face. At the daughter who'd come looking for a father she barely remembered.

"Sit down," Eluned said finally. "All of us. Sit."

It was a command, not a request. They sat—Eluned and Imogen on one side of the table, Mara on the other, the blue tin between them like something that could explode if handled wrong.

Eluned folded her hands on the table. Breathed in. Breathed out. When she spoke again her voice was calmer, more controlled, but Imogen could see the cost of that control in the tightness around her eyes.

"I'll tell you where he's buried. But first we need to talk about what happens next."

"I just want to visit his grave," Mara said. "That's all."

"Nothing is ever that simple." Eluned looked at Imogen. "She can stay three days? That's when her school trip ends?"

Imogen nodded.

"Fine. Three days. But if she stays, you open the letters. All of them. No more hiding behind arithmetic and excuses."

"Eluned—"

"All of them, Imogen. That's the deal. She wants to know about her father, and those letters are the only way she'll hear his voice. You want to know where he's buried, and I'll tell you. But you don't get to keep hiding. Not anymore. Not with her here."

The demand hung in the air between them. Imogen looked at the eleven unopened letters. At Mara's desperate hope. At Eluned's exhausted fury.

"I can't," Imogen said.

"Yes you can. You already opened one. You can open the rest."

"They're private—"

"He's been private for twenty years." Eluned's voice was gentle now, which made it worse. "Read them. Let us hear what he had to say. Maybe it'll help."

"Help with what?"

"Letting him go."

The words settled into the silence. Mara was watching Imogen with Thomas's eyes. Eluned was watching her with their mother's. And Imogen was trapped between them with eleven letters she'd spent twelve years avoiding and a promise she didn't know how to keep.

"One letter," she heard herself say. "I'll open one more. The second one. Today."

"All of them," Eluned insisted.

"I can't do all of them at once. One at a time. One per day until they're gone."

Eluned considered this. "Fine. One per day. Starting now."

She reached across the table and pushed the blue tin toward Imogen.

"Now?" Imogen's voice cracked.

"Right now. Both of us here. Both of us listening." Eluned looked at Mara. "Your father was my brother too. You're not the only one with questions."

Mara nodded slowly. "Then why won't anyone answer them?"

"Because some answers hurt more than the questions." Eluned's eyes were bright. "But maybe it's time to hurt a little if it means we stop hiding."

Imogen looked at the tin. At the second envelope, dated six months after the first. Six months of Thomas waiting for an answer. Six months of silence accumulating into years, into decades, into a lifetime of words she'd refused to hear.

Her hands shook as she reached for it.

The envelope was lighter than the first. Thinner. The paper had yellowed at the edges where twenty years had touched it. The postmark was from Cornwall, from a town Imogen had never visited even though Thomas had lived there for two decades. His handwriting on the front—her name in that impatient slant, the 'g' diving below the line like a gull diving below the water.

She counted to ten. Then twenty. Then thirty.

Eluned waited. Mara waited. The whole kitchen waited, heavy with the weight of words about to be spoken.

At fifty, Imogen stopped counting and opened the letter.

The paper tore along the seal. She pulled out a single page, folded once. Thomas's handwriting covered both sides—smaller than the first letter, more cramped, like he'd had more to say than space to say it in.

"Read it aloud," Eluned said quietly. "Both of you should hear it."

Imogen's throat closed. "It's private—"

"He's been private for twenty years. Read it."

Imogen looked at the first line. At Thomas's younger voice speaking across decades of silence. Her lips moved, counting the words before she could make herself say them aloud.

"Read it," Eluned said again.

Imogen read.

"Dear Imogen,

I know you probably won't answer this letter either, but I'm writing anyway because not writing feels like giving up and I'm not ready to give up on you yet.

It's been six months since I wrote the first letter. Six months in Cornwall, which is beautiful but lonely. I've got work at a boat yard—restoration mostly, old fishing vessels and pleasure boats that people bring in more broken than whole. The work is good. Keeps my hands busy. Keeps me from thinking too much about Wales, about you and Eluned, about everything I left behind.

The town is small. Everyone knows everyone. They know I'm from Wales, that I left home, but they don't ask too many questions and I don't offer too many answers. That suits me fine.

I've got a flat above the chandlery. Two rooms and a view of the harbor. There's a spare room if you ever wanted to visit. I know you won't, but I'm telling you anyway. The door's open. It'll stay open.

I think about you more than I probably should. Wonder if you're still teaching, if you've moved away from the house, if you think about me at all or if you've managed to forget I existed. I hope you haven't forgotten. I hope you're angry instead. Anger means you still feel something and feeling something is better than the arithmetic you hide behind.

I'm not angry anymore. I was for a while after I left—angry at you, at Eluned, at Mum for dying, at myself for not being able to fix it. But anger takes too much energy and I didn't have enough left after the leaving.

What I have now is hope. Stupid, probably. But I hope you'll write back. Hope you'll tell me how you are, what you're doing, if you've forgiven yourself yet for something that was never your fault.

I don't blame you. I told you that in the last letter but I'll say it again because I don't think you believed me. It wasn't your fault. The rain, the road, the way Mum didn't put her seatbelt on, the way I told you to go faster—none of that was your fault. But you've made it your fault anyway and I can't fix that from Cornwall. Only you can fix that.

I miss you. I miss my sister who used to count the stars with me. I miss the way you'd get so focused on a problem you'd forget to eat. I miss having someone who knew me before I became the person who left.

If you ever change your mind, the address is on the envelope. The spare room is waiting. I'll keep writing even if you never write back.

Your brother,
Thomas"

Imogen's voice broke on the last word. She set the letter down with shaking hands. Across the table, Mara's face was wet with tears. Beside her, Eluned had her eyes closed, her jaw tight.

"He invited you to visit," Mara said, her voice barely there. "Did you go?"

"No."

"Did you write back?"

"No. I never answered any of them."

The admission hung in the air, terrible and true. Twenty years of letters. Twenty years of silence. Twenty years of Thomas reaching out and Imogen refusing to reach back.

"Why?" Mara's voice cracked. "He wanted to know you. He missed you. Why wouldn't you answer?"

Because answering meant acknowledging what she'd done. Meant facing the guilt. Meant letting Thomas forgive her when she couldn't forgive herself. Because the arithmetic only worked if she kept all the terms on the left side of the equation, and Thomas's forgiveness would have unbalanced everything.

"I was afraid," Imogen said.

"Of what?"

"Of hearing his voice. Of him being kind. Of him forgiving me when I didn't deserve it."

Mara shook her head. "That's not a reason. That's an excuse."

She was right. Sixteen years old and seeing straight through to the truth Imogen had spent twenty years avoiding.

Eluned opened her eyes. Looked at Imogen with something that might have been pity or might have been recognition. "He kept the spare room for you. For twenty years. Even after you never came, never wrote, never gave him any reason to hope. He kept it ready."

"How do you know?"

"Because I went to Cornwall after he died. To handle his things, to meet with the solicitor, to tell his ex-wife what had happened. The flat was exactly like he described it in the letter. Two rooms and a view of the harbor. And the spare room had a bed made up with clean sheets, fresh towels in the bathroom, like he was expecting you to knock on the door any day."

Imogen couldn't breathe. The kitchen was too small. The three of them were too close. Thomas's words were too present, too alive, too much proof that he'd spent twenty years waiting for a sister who never came.

"I'm sorry," she whispered.

"Sorry doesn't help him." Eluned's voice was gentle but firm. "He's gone. But she's not." She nodded at Mara. "She's here asking the same questions he asked for twenty years. Wanting the same thing—to know her family. To understand where she came from."

Mara wiped her eyes. "I don't want to make this harder. I just wanted to see his grave. To stand there and tell him I knew he existed, that I'm trying to know him even though it's too late."

"It's not too late to know him." Eluned stood. Went to the counter. Poured herself tea from the pot that had gone cold. "That's what the letters are for. That's what we're for. His sisters. His daughter. We're what's left of him."

She turned back to the table. "Tomorrow we'll open the third letter. The next day, the fourth. By Sunday we'll have read them all and you'll have heard his voice and you'll know who your father was." She looked at Imogen. "And maybe we'll finally let him go."

Imogen looked at the letter on the table. At Thomas's handwriting, his words, his hope that had outlived him by twelve years. At Mara's grey eyes watching her with desperate need. At Eluned's brown eyes watching her with exhausted patience.

Three women in a kitchen too small for all their grief.

Three days to read eleven letters.

Ten more chances to hear Thomas's voice.

The arithmetic was impossible. But Imogen nodded anyway, because refusing meant sending Mara away and closing the tin and spending another twelve years frozen in a moment she couldn't count her way past.

"Okay," she said. "Okay."

"There's something else," Mara said quietly. "My mum told me he killed himself. That he went out in a boat in bad weather and didn't come back. She said it was suicide."

Eluned's face went very still. Imogen stopped breathing.

"Is that true?" Mara asked. "Did my dad kill himself?"

Eluned looked at Imogen. Imogen looked at the blue tin with its ten unopened letters, one of them the twelfth, the last one, the one that had arrived the day Thomas died.

"I don't know," Eluned said finally. "The coroner couldn't say for certain. He drowned. That's all we know."

"But the letters might say. The last one might explain."

"Maybe."

Mara nodded slowly. Wiped her eyes again. "Then I guess we keep reading."

* * *

Eluned stayed.

She made fresh tea. Made sandwiches neither Imogen nor Mara could eat. Cleared away the breakfast dishes and washed them with careful precision while Imogen and Mara sat at the table in silence.

Thomas's letter stayed on the table beside the first one. Two letters now, two pieces of Thomas's voice speaking across the years. Ten more waiting.

"I need to call the school," Imogen said finally. "Tell them I won't be in Monday either."

"Take the week," Eluned said from the sink. "Tell them it's a family emergency."

"It is a family emergency."

"Then tell them that."

Imogen pulled out her phone. Dialed. Helen answered on the second ring, her voice warm and concerned and exactly what Imogen needed to hear.

"Imogen! We've been worried. Are you all right?"

"I'm—" She looked at Mara, at Eluned, at the blue tin. "I'm dealing with something. A family matter. I need to take the rest of the week."

"Of course. Whatever you need. Do you want me to send work home?"

"No. I just need time."

"Take it. We'll manage. You take care of yourself."

Imogen hung up. Set the phone on the table. Looked at Eluned. "Where is he buried?"

Eluned dried her hands on the tea towel. Came back to the table. Sat.

"There's a cemetery in Cornwall. Small. Overlooks the sea. He's there."

"Can we visit?"

"It's six hours away."

"I have three days," Mara said. "We could drive down. See the grave. Come back."

Eluned shook her head. "Not yet. First we read the letters. All of them. Then we go to Cornwall together, the three of us, and we visit his grave and we say goodbye properly."

"Why do we have to wait?" Mara's frustration was building again, that sixteen-year-old impatience with adult logic.

"Because the letters will help you understand who he was. What he went through. What he wanted to say. And when you stand at his grave, you'll be able to tell him you heard his voice. That you listened."

Mara pressed her hands to her face. "This is so hard."

"I know."

"I didn't think it would be this hard."

"Grief never is what you think it'll be," Eluned said quietly. "It's always harder and longer and more complicated than anyone tells you."

She stood. "I need to go to work for a few hours. I'll be back tonight. We'll have dinner together, the three of us. Tomorrow we'll open the third letter."

"You're coming back?" Imogen asked.

"Did you think I'd leave you alone with this?"

"I thought you were angry."

"I am angry." Eluned's voice softened. "But I'm also your sister. And I'm tired of being angry alone while you count alone and we both pretend we're fine."

She picked up her coat. Her bag. Stopped at the door.

"Don't open any more letters without me. We do this together or not at all."

Then she was gone, the sound of her car fading down the road, and Imogen and Mara were alone again with two opened letters and ten more waiting and three days to read them all before Mara had to go home and face her mother and Imogen had to face what came after.

Mara stood. "Can I go for a walk? I need air."

"The flats are that way." Imogen pointed toward the window. "Follow the path. It's low tide. You can walk out as far as you want."

"Will you come?"

Imogen looked at the letters. At the blue tin. At the photograph of her mother watching from above the stove.

"Not right now. But you go. I'll be here when you get back."

Mara nodded. Got her too-thin coat. Walked out the door Eluned had just closed.

And Imogen sat alone in the kitchen counting the silence.

Two letters opened. Ten remaining. Three days. Seventy-two hours. Four thousand three hundred and twenty minutes until Mara left and the arithmetic returned to its familiar patterns.

But the patterns were already broken. The tin was open. Thomas's voice was in the room. Eluned was coming back. And somewhere out on the flats, a girl with grey eyes was walking toward the sea, counting her own grief in steps Imogen couldn't measure.

The tide was going out again, taking the flats with it, the way it always did.

Without asking anyone if they were ready.

Without waiting for the counting to stop.

Without needing the numbers to make sense.

The tiles were still grey and white and numbered exactly one thousand one hundred and seventy-six, though counting them this morning didn't bring the same relief it usually did.

She filled the kettle. Put bread in the toaster. Set out two cups, two plates. The arithmetic of breakfast for two people instead of one.

Mara appeared in the doorway wearing the same jeans from yesterday and a different shirt, her dark hair wet from the shower. Her grey eyes—Thomas's grey eyes—took in the kitchen, the careful preparation, Imogen's hands arranging things just so.

"Good morning," Mara said.

"Morning. Did you sleep?"

"Some. The bed's comfortable. Thank you."

The politeness was careful, practiced. Both of them performing normal. Both of them pretending this wasn't strange.

"Tea?" Imogen asked.

"Please. Can I help?"

"It's fine. The kettle's almost—" The kettle clicked off. "Ready."

Imogen poured. Her hands were steady. She counted the seconds of pouring. Four for each cup. Eight total. The steam rose in identical patterns, predictable and safe.

They sat at the table. The blue tin sat between them like a third presence, impossible to ignore. Mara's eyes kept going to it, then away, then back.

"Did you sleep?" Mara asked, echoing Imogen's question but making it mean something different. Did you sleep or did you stay awake thinking about the letters, about your promise, about how to fix this?

"Some," Imogen said, echoing Mara's answer.

The toast popped. Imogen got up, buttered it, brought it back. Mara took a piece and ate it in small, careful bites. Sixteen. Still a child in some ways, still learning how to take up space in the world.

"I texted my mum," Mara said. "Told her we got to London fine. That I forgot my charger."

"Three days?"

"That's when the trip ends. Sunday night."

Today was Friday. Three days. Seventy-two hours. Four thousand three hundred and twenty minutes. The numbers should have been comforting but they just felt like a countdown to something Imogen wasn't ready for.

"What happens Sunday night?"

Mara shrugged. "I go home. Or I tell her the truth. Haven't decided yet."

Her voice was casual but her hands were tight around the tea cup, her knuckles white. Imogen recognized that grip. That was someone holding on because letting go meant falling apart.

"You could call her. Tell her you're safe."

"She'd make me come home."

"She's probably worried."

"She's always worried. That's what she does." Mara set down the cup. "I'm not going back until I know where he is. I need to see where they buried him."

The determination in her voice was so much like Thomas it hurt. Thomas deciding to leave Wales. Thomas deciding to keep writing even when Imogen never wrote back. Thomas deciding to rebuild the boat from their childhood even though he'd never finished it.

"I'll call Eluned this morning," Imogen said. "I promise."

Mara nodded. Looked at the blue tin. "Are you going to open another one?"

"I don't know."

"Why did you open the first one? After twelve years, why now?"

Because you called. Because your voice asking about Thomas broke something in Imogen's careful architecture. Because the arithmetic of avoidance had finally accumulated enough weight to collapse under itself.

"It was time," Imogen said, which wasn't an answer but was all she had.

Her phone buzzed on the counter. They both looked at it. Imogen's stomach tightened. It could be the school. Could be Eluned. Could be nothing important, just a reminder or a notification, but her body responded to it the way you respond to a fire alarm—immediate, visceral, counting the seconds until it stops.

She crossed to the phone. Checked it.

Five missed calls from Eluned. Three from yesterday. Two from this morning. No messages. Just the calls, insistent and unanswered.

"Is it her?" Mara asked. "Your sister?"

"Yes."

"Are you going to call her back?"

Imogen looked at the phone in her hand. At the five missed calls that were really five chances to ask the question she should have asked twelve years ago. Five chances to find out where Thomas was buried. Five chances to stop being the sister who was too careful to fall apart.

"Yes," she said. "I will."

But not yet. Not with Mara watching. Not with the blue tin open and the morning still too new and her counting already spiraling past fifty, sixty, seventy because Eluned's calls meant Eluned was worried or angry or both and Imogen didn't know how to face that yet.

The sound of tires on gravel made them both look toward the window.

Imogen knew that sound. Knew the particular crunch of Eluned's car pulling up to the house. Knew what it meant that Eluned hadn't waited for Imogen to call back but had come instead.

"Is that—" Mara started.

"Yes."

Imogen set down her phone. Her heart was beating too fast, that familiar flutter of panic when things moved faster than she could count, faster than she could control. She pressed her hands flat against the table. One thousand one hundred and seventy-six tiles. The blue tin. Eleven unopened letters. One niece with grey eyes. One sister pulling up outside.

The car door slammed.

Footsteps on the gravel. Quick, determined. Not the careful footsteps of someone who's uncertain. The footsteps of someone who's decided something and come to make it happen.

Mara stood. "Should I—"

"Stay." Imogen's voice came out sharper than she meant it. "Please. Just stay."

The knock came. Three sharp raps on the door.

Imogen didn't count her steps this time. Just crossed to the door and opened it.

Eluned stood on the doorstep wearing her work coat and her brown eyes already searching past Imogen into the house, looking for whatever had made Imogen ignore five phone calls. Her hair was pulled back, still damp like she'd come straight from the shower. Her jaw was tight the way it got when she was trying to hold something in.

"You didn't answer," Eluned said.

"I know. I was going to call—"

"I've been worried. After the other night, after what I said, I thought—" She stopped. Her eyes had found Mara standing in the kitchen doorway. "Who is that?"

The question came out flat. Careful. Eluned's voice when she already knew the answer but needed to hear it said aloud.

Imogen's mouth went dry. "Her name is Mara."

"Mara."

"Thomas's daughter."

Eluned went very still. Her eyes moved from Mara to Imogen and back again, taking it in—the girl in the kitchen, the overnight bag visible in the hallway, the two cups on the table, the whole impossible situation that Imogen had created without asking, without warning, without thinking about what it would do to Eluned to walk in and find Thomas's daughter here.

"When did she—"

"Yesterday. She called, then she came. She had nowhere else to go."

Eluned's jaw tightened further. She stepped inside, closed the door behind her with careful precision. Walked past Imogen into the kitchen where Mara stood very straight, very still, trying to look older than sixteen and not quite managing it.

"Hello," Mara said. Her voice was steady but her hands had found each other, fingers lacing tight. "I'm Mara Penrose. You're Eluned?"

"I am." Eluned set her bag on the counter. Took off her coat. Each movement deliberate, controlled. "Does your mother know you're here?"

"She thinks I'm in London. School trip."

"So that's a no."

"I needed to find out where my dad is buried. No one would tell me."

Eluned looked at Imogen. "And you let her stay."

It wasn't a question. It was an accusation wrapped in four quiet words.

"She had nowhere to go," Imogen said. "She came all the way from Cornwall—"

"So you brought her into this." Eluned gestured at the table, at the blue tin, at the letters spread across Imogen's carefully constructed solitude. "After everything I said the other night. After I told you those letters would destroy you. You opened one and then brought his daughter here to witness it."

"I didn't plan—"

"You never plan. You just react. You just let things happen to you and then count your way through the wreckage."

The words landed like blows. Mara shifted her weight, uncomfortable, caught in the middle of something she didn't understand.

"I should go," Mara said quietly. "I can find somewhere else—"

"No." Imogen's voice surprised her, sharp and certain. "You're staying. I promised I'd help you and I will."

Eluned laughed, but there was no humor in it. "You promised. Like you promised to deal with the letters twelve years ago? Like you promised to talk to me about Thomas before now?"

"That's not fair."

"Fair?" Eluned's control cracked, just for a moment, her voice rising. "You want to talk about fair? I handled everything when he died. The funeral, the arrangements, the phone calls to his ex-wife telling her that Thomas was gone and yes, we'd make sure Mara was taken care of financially but no, Imogen wasn't in a state to meet her. I handled all of it while you stayed here counting tiles and refusing to open his letters. And now you've dragged this girl into it because she asked you a question you should have asked me twelve years ago."

The silence that followed was absolute. Mara's face had gone white. Imogen couldn't breathe, couldn't count, couldn't do anything except stand there with the truth of Eluned's words settling into her chest like stones.

"I'm sorry," Imogen whispered.

"Sorry doesn't help her." Eluned nodded at Mara. "Sorry doesn't tell her where her father is buried. Sorry doesn't give her twelve years back."

"Then tell me." Mara's voice cut through the tension, young and desperate and demanding. "Please. You know where he is. Just tell me."

Eluned looked at her for a long moment. At Thomas's grey eyes in Mara's young face. At the daughter who'd come looking for a father she barely remembered.

"Sit down," Eluned said finally. "All of us. Sit."

It was a command, not a request. They sat—Eluned and Imogen on one side of the table, Mara on the other, the blue tin between them like something that could explode if handled wrong.

Eluned folded her hands on the table. Breathed in. Breathed out. When she spoke again her voice was calmer, more controlled, but Imogen could see the cost of that control in the tightness around her eyes.

"Three days. That's when your school trip ends?"

Mara nodded.

"If you stay, Imogen opens the letters. All of them. One per day." Eluned looked at Imogen. "No more hiding behind arithmetic and excuses."

"Eluned—"

"That's the deal. She wants to know about her father, and those letters are the only way she'll hear his voice. You want to know where he's buried, and I'll tell you." Her voice was gentle now, which made it worse. "But you don't get to keep hiding. Not anymore. Not with her here."

Imogen looked at the eleven unopened letters. At Mara's grey eyes. At Eluned's exhausted fury.

"One letter per day," she said quietly. "Starting now."

Eluned reached across the table and pushed the blue tin toward Imogen. "Now."

Imogen's hands shook as she reached for the second envelope. The paper had yellowed at the edges where twenty years had touched it. The postmark was from Cornwall, from a town Imogen had never visited even though Thomas had lived there for two decades. His handwriting on the front—her name in that impatient slant, the 'g' diving below the line like a gull diving below the water.

She counted to ten. Then twenty. Then thirty.

Eluned waited. Mara waited. The whole kitchen waited, heavy with the weight of words about to be spoken.

At fifty, Imogen stopped counting and opened the letter.

The paper tore along the seal. She pulled out a single page, folded once. Thomas's handwriting covered both sides—smaller than the first letter, more cramped, like he'd had more to say than space to say it in.

"Read it aloud," Eluned said quietly. "Both of you should hear it."

Imogen's throat closed. "It's private—"

"He's been private for twenty years. Read it."

Imogen looked at the first line. At Thomas's younger voice speaking across decades of silence. Her lips moved, counting the words before she could make herself say them aloud.

"Read it," Eluned said again.

Imogen read.

"Dear Imogen,

I know you probably won't answer this letter either, but I'm writing anyway because not writing feels like giving up and I'm not ready to give up on you yet.

It's been six months since I wrote the first letter. Six months in Cornwall, which is beautiful but lonely. I've got work at a boat yard—restoration mostly, old fishing vessels and pleasure boats that people bring in more broken than whole. The work is good. Keeps my hands busy. Keeps me from thinking too much about Wales, about you and Eluned, about everything I left behind.

The town is small. Everyone knows everyone. They know I'm from Wales, that I left home, but they don't ask too many questions and I don't offer too many answers. That suits me fine.

I've got a flat above the chandlery. Two rooms and a view of the harbor. There's a spare room if you ever wanted to visit. I know you won't, but I'm telling you anyway. The door's open. It'll stay open.

I think about you more than I probably should. Wonder if you're still teaching, if you've moved away from the house, if you think about me at all or if you've managed to forget I existed. I hope you haven't forgotten. I hope you're angry instead. Anger means you still feel something and feeling something is better than the arithmetic you hide behind.

I'm not angry anymore. I was for a while after I left—angry at you, at Eluned, at Mum for dying, at myself for not being able to fix it. But anger takes too much energy and I didn't have enough left after the leaving.

What I have now is hope. Stupid, probably. But I hope you'll write back. Hope you'll tell me how you are, what you're doing, if you've forgiven yourself yet for something that was never your fault.

I don't blame you. I told you that in the last letter but I'll say it again because I don't think you believed me. It wasn't your fault. The rain, the road, the way Mum didn't put her seatbelt on, the way I told you to go faster—none of that was your fault. But you've made it your fault anyway and I can't fix that from Cornwall. Only you can fix that.

I miss you. I miss my sister who used to count the stars with me. I miss the way you'd get so focused on a problem you'd forget to eat. I miss having someone who knew me before I became the person who left.

If you ever change your mind, the address is on the envelope. The spare room is waiting. I'll keep writing even if you never write back.

Your brother,
Thomas"

Imogen's voice broke on the last word. She set the letter down with shaking hands. Across the table, Mara's face was wet with tears. Beside her, Eluned had her eyes closed, her jaw tight.

"He invited you to visit," Mara said, her voice barely there. "Did you go?"

"No."

"Did you write back?"

"No. I never answered any of them."

The admission hung in the air, terrible and true. Twenty years of letters. Twenty years of silence. Twenty years of Thomas reaching out and Imogen refusing to reach back.

"Why?" Mara's voice cracked. "He wanted to know you. He missed you. Why wouldn't you answer?"

Because answering meant acknowledging what she'd done. Meant facing the guilt. Meant letting Thomas forgive her when she couldn't forgive herself. Because the arithmetic only worked if she kept all the terms on the left side of the equation, and Thomas's forgiveness would have unbalanced everything.

"I was afraid," Imogen said.

"Of what?"

"Of hearing his voice. Of him being kind. Of him forgiving me when I didn't deserve it."

Mara shook her head. "That's not a reason. That's an excuse."

She was right. Sixteen years old and seeing straight through to the truth Imogen had spent twenty years avoiding.

Eluned opened her eyes. Looked at Imogen with something that might have been pity or might have been recognition. "He kept the spare room for you. For twenty years. Even after you never came, never wrote, never gave him any reason to hope. He kept it ready."

"How do you know?"

"Because I went to Cornwall after he died. To handle his things, to meet with the solicitor, to tell his ex-wife what had happened. The flat was exactly like he described it in the letter. Two rooms and a view of the harbor. And the spare room had a bed made up with clean sheets, fresh towels in the bathroom, like he was expecting you to knock on the door any day."

Imogen couldn't breathe. The kitchen was too small. The three of them were too close. Thomas's words were too present, too alive, too much proof that he'd spent twenty years waiting for a sister who never came.

"I'm sorry," she whispered.

"Sorry doesn't help him." Eluned's voice was gentle but firm. "He's gone. But she's not." She nodded at Mara. "She's here asking the same questions he asked for twenty years. Wanting the same thing—to know her family. To understand where she came from."

Mara wiped her eyes. "I don't want to make this harder. I just wanted to see his grave. To stand there and tell him I knew he existed, that I'm trying to know him even though it's too late."

"It's not too late to know him." Eluned stood. Went to the counter. Poured herself tea from the pot that had gone cold. "That's what the letters are for. That's what we're for. His sisters. His daughter. We're what's left of him."

She turned back to the table. "Tomorrow we'll open the third letter. The next day, the fourth. By Sunday we'll have read them all and you'll have heard his voice and you'll know who your father was." She looked at Imogen. "And maybe we'll finally let him go."

Imogen looked at the letter on the table. At Thomas's handwriting, his words, his hope that had outlived him by twelve years. At Mara's grey eyes watching her with desperate need. At Eluned's brown eyes watching her with exhausted patience.

Three women in a kitchen too small for all their grief.

Three days to read eleven letters.

Ten more chances to hear Thomas's voice.

The arithmetic was impossible. But Imogen nodded anyway, because refusing meant sending Mara away and closing the tin and spending another twelve years frozen in a moment she couldn't count her way past.

"Okay," she said. "Okay."

"There's something else," Mara said quietly. "My mum told me he killed himself. That he went out in a boat in bad weather and didn't come back. She said it was suicide."

Eluned's face went very still. Imogen stopped breathing.

"Is that true?" Mara asked. "Did my dad kill himself?"

Eluned looked at Imogen. Imogen looked at the blue tin with its ten unopened letters, one of them the twelfth, the last one, the one that had arrived the day Thomas died.

"I don't know," Eluned said finally. "The coroner couldn't say for certain. He drowned. That's all we know."

"But the letters might say. The last one might explain."

"Maybe."

Mara nodded slowly. Wiped her eyes again. "Then I guess we keep reading."

* * *

Eluned stayed.

She made fresh tea. Made sandwiches neither Imogen nor Mara could eat. Cleared away the breakfast dishes and washed them with careful precision while Imogen and Mara sat at the table in silence.

Thomas's letter stayed on the table beside the first one. Two letters now, two pieces of Thomas's voice speaking across the years. Ten more waiting.

"I need to call the school," Imogen said finally. "Tell them I won't be in Monday either."

"Take the week," Eluned said from the sink. "Tell them it's a family emergency."

"It is a family emergency."

"Then tell them that."

Imogen pulled out her phone. Dialed. Helen answered on the second ring, her voice warm and concerned and exactly what Imogen needed to hear.

"Imogen! We've been worried. Are you all right?"

"I'm—" She looked at Mara, at Eluned, at the blue tin. "I'm dealing with something. A family matter. I need to take the rest of the week."

"Of course. Whatever you need. Do you want me to send work home?"

"No. I just need time."

"Take it. We'll manage. You take care of yourself."

Imogen hung up. Set the phone on the table. Looked at Eluned. "Where is he buried?"

Eluned dried her hands on the tea towel. Came back to the table. Sat.

"There's a cemetery in Cornwall. Small. Overlooks the sea. He's there."

"Can we visit?"

"It's six hours away."

"I have three days," Mara said. "We could drive down. See the grave. Come back."

Eluned shook her head. "Not yet. First we read the letters. All of them. Then we go to Cornwall together, the three of us, and we visit his grave and we say goodbye properly."

"Why do we have to wait?" Mara's frustration was building again, that sixteen-year-old impatience with adult logic.

"Because the letters will help you understand who he was. What he went through. What he wanted to say. And when you stand at his grave, you'll be able to tell him you heard his voice. That you listened."

Mara pressed her hands to her face. "This is so hard."

"I know."

"I didn't think it would be this hard."

"Grief never is what you think it'll be," Eluned said quietly. "It's always harder and longer and more complicated than anyone tells you."

She stood. "I need to go to work for a few hours. I'll be back tonight. We'll have dinner together, the three of us. Tomorrow we'll open the third letter."

"You're coming back?" Imogen asked.

"Did you think I'd leave you alone with this?"

"I thought you were angry."

"I am angry." Eluned's voice softened. "But I'm also your sister. And I'm tired of being angry alone while you count alone and we both pretend we're fine."

She picked up her coat. Her bag. Stopped at the door.

"Don't open any more letters without me. We do this together or not at all."

Then she was gone, the sound of her car fading down the road, and Imogen and Mara were alone again with two opened letters and ten more waiting and three days to read them all before Mara had to go home and face her mother and Imogen had to face what came after.

Mara stood. "Can I go for a walk? I need air."

"The flats are that way." Imogen pointed toward the window. "Follow the path. It's low tide. You can walk out as far as you want."

"Will you come?"

Imogen looked at the letters. At the blue tin. At the photograph of her mother watching from above the stove.

"Not right now. But you go. I'll be here when you get back."

Mara nodded. Got her too-thin coat. Walked out the door Eluned had just closed.

And Imogen sat alone in the kitchen counting the silence.

Two letters opened. Ten remaining. Three days. Seventy-two hours. Four thousand three hundred and twenty minutes until Mara left and the arithmetic returned to its familiar patterns.

But the patterns were already broken. The tin was open. Thomas's voice was in the room. Eluned was coming back. And somewhere out on the flats, a girl with grey eyes was walking toward the sea, counting her own grief in steps Imogen couldn't measure.

The tide was going out again, taking the flats with it, the way it always did.

Without asking anyone if they were ready.

Without waiting for the counting to stop.

Without needing the numbers to make sense.
